reading.h: What a DPP is, and its one advantage
reading.body:
A **direct participation program (DPP)** is a business venture — usually a **limited partnership** — that **passes income, gains, losses, deductions, and credits straight through** to investors. There is no entity-level tax; each investor gets a **Schedule K-1** and reports a share of the results.

The single feature that sets a DPP apart from a REIT or a corporation is the **flow-through of losses**. A corporation traps its losses at the entity level and a REIT cannot pass losses through at all; a DPP hands them to the investors. That is the whole reason high-bracket investors with passive income use them — and the reason a DPP is unsuitable for a low-bracket investor or a retirement account.

reading.h: GP vs. LP — the liability line
reading.body:
The **general partner (GP)** runs the business, owes a **fiduciary duty** to the limited partners, keeps at least a 1% interest, and carries **unlimited personal liability**.

The **limited partners (LPs)** put up the capital and stay **passive**. Their liability is **limited to what they invested plus any recourse debt they personally signed for**. LPs may vote on major matters (dissolve the partnership, sell assets, remove the GP) and inspect the books — but if an LP starts **participating in management, they risk losing their limited liability**. In a dissolution, the priority order is secured creditors, then general/unsecured creditors, then **limited partners, then general partners** — LPs rank ahead of GPs.

reading.h: The three documents and becoming an LP
reading.body:
Three documents build a limited partnership. The **certificate of limited partnership** is filed with the state and names the GP, the business, and the capital. The **partnership agreement** sets out rights, duties, the profit split, and the GP's powers. The **subscription agreement** is what the investor signs to apply — it states the investor's net worth and income, affirms they understand the risks, and grants the GP power of attorney.

The timing point the exam loves: an investor becomes a limited partner **only when the GP signs and accepts** the subscription agreement — not when the investor signs it.

DPP interests are sold **public** (registered, with a prospectus) or by **private placement** (Reg D, accredited investors). Under **FINRA Rule 2310**, total **organization and offering expenses are capped at 15% of gross proceeds**, and **underwriting compensation is capped at 10%**. Before recommending a DPP, a rep must gather the customer's **income, net worth, and tax-bracket** data — suitability here is strict because of illiquidity and complexity.

A program is called a **"blind pool"** when a large share of proceeds is raised for **unspecified** properties or projects, so investors are betting on the GP rather than on named assets.

reading.h: Program types and their tax deductions
reading.body:
**Real estate:** **raw land** is pure appreciation — **no depreciation, no income, most speculative**; **existing properties** give immediate cash flow and depreciation (most conservative); **new construction** carries cost-overrun risk. Depreciation runs straight-line over **27.5 years** (residential) or **39 years** (commercial); **land is never depreciable**.

**Oil and gas:** **exploratory (wildcat)** drilling is the **highest risk and offers the largest first-year deductions** through **intangible drilling costs (IDCs)** — labor, fuel, site prep, deductible in the year incurred whether or not the well produces. **Income (stripper)** programs buy producing wells for immediate, lower-risk cash flow. Oil and gas is the **only** DPP in which **nonrecourse debt does NOT add to basis** (in real estate, qualified nonrecourse financing does).

reading.h: Passive losses, basis, and phantom income
reading.body:
DPP income and losses are **passive**, so a passive loss can offset **only passive income** (from other DPPs or rental real estate) — **never** wages (active) or interest, dividends, and capital gains (portfolio). Unused passive losses **carry forward** and are released when the interest is fully disposed of.

Worked example: an investor with a $150,000 salary, $5,000 of dividends, and $4,000 of income from another partnership is allocated a $10,000 DPP loss. Only **$4,000** (against the passive partnership income) is deductible this year; the other **$6,000 is suspended** and carried forward.

Other mechanics: **basis** = cash invested + share of recourse debt + income − distributions − losses, and losses are deductible only up to basis (**at-risk rules**). The **crossover point** is when a program's taxable income first exceeds its deductions, producing **phantom income** — taxable income without matching cash. On sale, depreciation is **recaptured** as ordinary income.

A **REIT** owns or finances income-producing real estate; its shares are registered under the **1933 Act** (not the 1940 Act). **Listed REITs** trade on exchanges (liquid); **non-traded REITs** are illiquid, high-commission, and a FINRA sales-practice focus.

To qualify under IRC §856, a REIT must invest **≥75%** of assets in real estate, earn **≥75%** of gross income from real estate, and **distribute ≥90% of its taxable income** — then it deducts dividends paid, like a conduit. Distributions are mostly **ordinary income** (with a 20% §199A deduction). The exam's key contrast: a **REIT does NOT pass through losses** — that flow-through belongs to DPPs alone. A REIT is not a DPP and not an investment company.

flashcards.front: DPP's one advantage over a REIT or corporation
flashcards.back: Flow-through of LOSSES to investors (via Schedule K-1). A REIT passes through income but NOT losses.
GP: unlimited personal liability + fiduciary duty. LP: limited to investment plus any recourse debt personally signed.

flashcards.front: When does an investor become a limited partner?
flashcards.back: When the GP signs/accepts the subscription agreement — not when the investor signs it.
Certificate of limited partnership (filed with state), partnership agreement, subscription agreement.
Organization & offering expenses ≤ 15% of gross proceeds; underwriting compensation ≤ 10%.
Only passive income (other DPPs, rental real estate). NOT wages (active) or interest/dividends/gains (portfolio). Excess carries forward.

flashcards.front: Which DPP gives the largest first-year deductions and highest risk?
flashcards.back: Exploratory (wildcat) oil & gas, via intangible drilling costs (IDCs) deductible in year one.
None — land is never depreciable; raw land is pure appreciation, no income, most speculative.
Oil & gas: nonrecourse debt does NOT add to basis. Real estate: qualified nonrecourse financing DOES add to basis.
75% assets in real estate, 75% income from real estate, distribute 90% of taxable income; 100 holders; 5/50 rule.
Crossover = year taxable income first exceeds deductions; phantom income = taxable income without matching cash.
Secured creditors → general/unsecured creditors → limited partners → general partners.

quiz.stem: A limited partner invests $25,000 in a real estate limited partnership. The partnership later defaults on $2 million it borrowed. The limited partner's maximum possible loss is:
options: $25,000 plus a proportional share of the $2 million
Unlimited, the same as the general partner
Zero, because the general partner must absorb losses
$25,000, unless she personally signed for any of the partnership's debt
quiz.explanation: A limited partner's liability is capped at the amount invested plus any recourse debt she personally signed for. The general partner carries unlimited personal liability; a limited partner does not share the partnership's borrowings beyond her investment.

quiz.stem: An investor has a $150,000 salary, $5,000 of dividend income, and $4,000 of income from a real estate limited partnership. This year she is allocated a $10,000 loss from an oil and gas drilling program. The amount of that loss she may deduct this year is:
quiz.explanation: DPP losses are passive and may offset only passive income — not the salary (active) or dividends (portfolio). The $4,000 of partnership income is passive, so $4,000 is deductible; the remaining $6,000 is suspended and carried forward until she has passive income or disposes of the interest.

quiz.stem: The primary tax advantage a direct participation program offers that a REIT does NOT is:
options: Tax-free distributions to investors
The flow-through of losses to investors
Exemption from all federal income tax
A guaranteed 90% distribution of income
quiz.explanation: A DPP passes losses through to investors on a Schedule K-1; a REIT passes income through but cannot pass through losses. Neither vehicle makes distributions tax-free, and the 90% distribution is a REIT qualification test, not a DPP advantage.

quiz.stem: An investor signs and submits a subscription agreement for a limited partnership interest. The investor formally becomes a limited partner when:
options: The investor signs the subscription agreement
The general partner signs and accepts the subscription agreement
The certificate of limited partnership is filed with the state
The first cash distribution is paid
quiz.explanation: An investor becomes a limited partner only when the general partner signs and accepts the subscription agreement. The investor's signature is an application; the GP's acceptance completes admission.

quiz.stem: Under FINRA Rule 2310, total organization and offering expenses in a direct participation program are limited to what percentage of gross proceeds?
quiz.explanation: Rule 2310 caps organization and offering expenses at 15% of gross proceeds, with underwriting compensation separately capped at 10%. The 8.5% figure is the mutual-fund maximum sales charge, a different rule.

quiz.stem: An investor seeking the LARGEST first-year deductions and willing to accept the HIGHEST risk should be shown which DPP?
options: An existing-property real estate program
An income (stripper-well) oil and gas program
An exploratory (wildcat) oil and gas program
A raw-land real estate program
quiz.explanation: Exploratory (wildcat) drilling carries the highest risk and generates the largest intangible drilling cost (IDC) deductions in year one. Existing-property and income programs are more conservative, and raw land produces no deductions at all (land is not depreciable).

quiz.stem: Which statement about REITs is TRUE?
options: A REIT passes operating losses through to its shareholders
A REIT must distribute at least 90% of its taxable income to avoid entity-level tax on distributed income
A REIT is registered as an investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940
REIT distributions are generally tax-free to shareholders
quiz.explanation: A qualifying REIT distributes at least 90% of taxable income and deducts dividends paid, acting as a conduit. It is registered under the 1933 Act (not the 1940 Act), its distributions are mostly ordinary income, and — unlike a DPP — it cannot pass losses through to shareholders.

quiz.stem: In an oil and gas direct participation program, nonrecourse debt taken on by the partnership:
options: Increases each limited partner's basis, just as it does in a real estate program
Does not add to a limited partner's basis, unlike qualified nonrecourse financing in real estate
Is treated as a distribution to the limited partners
Converts the limited partners into general partners
quiz.explanation: Oil and gas is the only DPP in which nonrecourse debt does not add to a limited partner's basis. In a real estate program, qualified nonrecourse financing does add to basis, which is why the contrast is tested.
